title: Checks-Effects-Interactions (CEI) is the safe default for external calls
mechanism: Updating all state (effects) before any external interaction means a re-entrant caller observes already-finalized state, so recursion cannot double-spend.
required_assumptions: the state read by the check is the same state mutated by the effect
all value-bearing state is updated before the call
the call target is arbitrary (so reentrancy is possible without a guard)
why_safe: On re-entry, the caller sees balances already decremented, so a second withdraw fails the check; no state to double-spend.
known_limitations: does not protect read-only reentrancy where a VIEW function is re-entered mid-state-change and consumed by another contract
does not protect against cross-contract state corruption if a shared dependency is mutated during the call
gas cost of the call can still brick batch loops (use pull-payments)
fp_patterns: an external call at the END of a function with all state already updated is NOT reentrancy-vulnerable
a state update AFTER a call is the FP trigger — report only when state that matters to a later/recursive path is stale
evidence_required: show the state WRITE that occurs after the external call AND is reachable during a callback (a real re-entry entrypoint)
or show a view read consumed by another contract during the mutation window (read-only reentrancy)
mere presence of call()/transfer() is NOT evidence
verification_evidence: Solidity docs security-considerations; reproduce CEI-satisfying code with a reentrant attacker and assert the second call reverts.
root_cause: Unsafe variant of this pattern (state-after-call, no guard, unchecked result, unguarded privilege, no domain/nonce, non-atomic init, or unverified upgrade target) is what produces the vulnerability; the SAFE version shown here is the negative/FP reference.
preconditions: the code under audit implements the safe pattern shown (this is the false-positive reference)
no deviation from the required assumptions listed
impact: None when the pattern is followed correctly — this record is a FALSE-POSITIVE reference: matching this safe shape is not a vulnerability.
remediation: No remediation needed for code matching this safe pattern; only report when the code deviates from the required assumptions and the evidence_required criteria are met.

title: ReentrancyGuard is safe when applied to every state-touching entry
mechanism: A nonReentrant modifier sets a sentinel before executing and clears it after; a re-entrant call sees the sentinel and reverts, so the guarded function cannot be re-entered.
safe_code:
bool private _locked;
modifier nonReentrant() { require(!_locked, 'reentrant'); _locked = true; _; _locked = false; }
required_assumptions: the guard is applied to EVERY function that touches the shared state (not just the primary one)
the sentinel write itself is a state write that persists across the call (it is, in storage)
no unguarded function re-enters the same state
why_safe: Re-entry reverts at the sentinel check before any state effect can run twice.
known_limitations: only protects the guarded functions — an unguarded sibling sharing state is still exploitable (cross-function reentrancy)
does not protect read-only reentrancy consumed by OTHER contracts (the view is not guarded for readers)
storage-write-based guard means a transient-storage or memory-only pattern is different
fp_patterns: a guard present on the only state-writing function with no other writer is safe
an unguarded VIEW that does not mutate state is NOT a reentrancy hole by itself
evidence_required: to report: an unguarded function that mutates the same state OR a consumer reading guarded state mid-call
guards present on all writers is a negative finding (do not report)
verification_evidence: OZ audit history; Foundry: reentrant call reverts when guarded.
root_cause: Unsafe variant of this pattern (state-after-call, no guard, unchecked result, unguarded privilege, no domain/nonce, non-atomic init, or unverified upgrade target) is what produces the vulnerability; the SAFE version shown here is the negative/FP reference.

source: OpenZeppelin access control + Solidity docs — own words
title: Access control (onlyOwner/roles) is the safe default for privileged functions
mechanism: Restricting privileged functions with an owner/role check means only authorized callers can mint/set/sweep/upgrade.
safe_code:
modifier onlyOwner() { require(msg.sender == owner, 'not owner'); _; }
function setFee(uint f) external onlyOwner { fee = f; }
required_assumptions: owner/role is set atomically at construction/initialization (not left to a later unguarded setter)
the role check compares msg.sender (not an attacker-influenced value)
no path that bypasses the modifier (internal call without it, selfdestruct-created ownership)
why_safe: Only the authorized principal can execute the guarded branch; the check runs before effects.
known_limitations: does not protect against the owner key being compromised (that is a key-management issue, not a code flaw)
two-step ownership transfer is recommended to avoid accidental lockout
does not protect privileged-state reads consumed by others
fp_patterns: an external function with onlyOwner is NOT a vulnerability simply because it is callable
a public view returning owner data is not a privilege issue
a function callable by 'anyone' is a finding ONLY if its effect is privileged (mint/upgrade/sweep)
evidence_required: to report missing access control: show a state-changing function with a privileged effect and NO caller check
an intentional public function (e.g. deposit) is not a finding
verification_evidence: OZ docs; reproduce by calling the privileged fn from a non-owner and asserting revert.
root_cause: Unsafe variant of this pattern (state-after-call, no guard, unchecked result, unguarded privilege, no domain/nonce, non-atomic init, or unverified upgrade target) is what produces the vulnerability; the SAFE version shown here is the negative/FP reference.

source: OpenZeppelin SafeERC20 + Solidity docs — own words
title: Safe token transfers (SafeERC20) handle non-standard tokens
mechanism: SafeERC20 wraps transfer/transferFrom/approve with a success-bool check and a fallback for tokens that do not return a bool, so silent failures cannot leave the ledger inconsistent.
required_assumptions: the token contract actually implements transfer/transferFrom semantics (reverts or returns bool)
the wrapper is used for ALL token interactions (not just some)
approve is set to 0 first for tokens needing it (USDT-style) when changing non-zero allowance
why_safe: A failed transfer reverts (or the missing-return fallback still validates), so state is not mutated on failure.
known_limitations: does not handle fee-on-transfer/deflationary tokens (balance-delta must be measured separately)
does not protect against malicious token contracts (only non-standard, non-malicious ones)
safeApprove on a non-zero allowance can fail for USDT-like tokens (use safeIncreaseAllowance)
fp_patterns: a plain transfer() WITHOUT checking the return is a finding only when the token is non-standard or the call can silently fail
a require(ok) on the return bool is safe
safetransfer from a standard ERC20 that always returns true is safe even without SafeERC20
evidence_required: to report: show a transfer whose return is unchecked AND a state mutation after it (or a fee/deflation token integration)
a checked call with require(ok) is a negative finding
verification_evidence: OZ SafeERC20 docs; Foundry: a no-return-bool token fails without the wrapper, succeeds with it.

source: Solidity 0.8 checked arithmetic + SafeMath docs — own words
title: Safe arithmetic: Solidity 0.8 checked math / SafeMath / overflow guards
mechanism: Solidity >=0.8 reverts on overflow/underflow by default; SafeMath (or explicit checks) provides the same guarantee on older compilers, so arithmetic cannot silently wrap.
required_assumptions: all arithmetic uses checked math (0.8 default, or SafeMath everywhere)
no unchecked{} block around value-bearing math
the compiler version is actually >=0.8 for the deployed code
why_safe: Overflow/underflow reverts rather than wrapping, so balances/limits cannot silently flip.
known_limitations: unchecked{} blocks intentionally bypass checks (used for gas) — each must be proven safe
division/truncation rounding is NOT protected by overflow checks (separate class)
SafeMath only helps where it is actually used
fp_patterns: arithmetic on 0.8 code without unchecked is NOT an overflow finding (compiler reverts)
unchecked{} is a finding only when the bounded values are not proven within range
a subtraction inside a require(x >= y) guard is safe
evidence_required: to report: show an unchecked{} or pre-0.8 bare operation on user-influenced values that can exceed the type range
plain 0.8 checked math with no unchecked is a negative finding
verification_evidence: Solidity 0.8 release notes; Foundry: a+b overflows and reverts on 0.8, wraps on 0.7.
root_cause: Unsafe variant of this pattern (state-after-call, no guard, unchecked result, unguarded privilege, no domain/nonce, non-atomic init, or unverified upgrade target) is what produces the vulnerability; the SAFE version shown here is the negative/FP reference.

title: Initialization protection (initializer modifier + _disableInitializers)
mechanism: An initializer modifier tracks a bool so initialize() can run exactly once; upgradeable implementations disable initialization in their constructor so the implementation itself cannot be front-run-initialized.
required_assumptions: initialize() is the ONLY way to set privileged storage
the proxy is initialized atomically (same tx as deploy, or by a trusted script before use)
the implementation constructor calls _disableInitializers()
why_safe: Once initialized, re-initialization reverts; the implementation deployed standalone can never be taken over via initialize().
known_limitations: protects the implementation from direct-init takeover, but the PROXY must still be initialized before first use (or an attacker initializes the proxy itself)
does not protect against a proxy deployed and left uninitialized
constructor-vs-initialize storage layout must still be correct
fp_patterns: a proxy that initializes atomically at deploy is NOT vulnerable to init front-running
initialize() with the initializer modifier is safe
a plain initialize() WITHOUT a guard on a deployed-not-yet-initialized proxy IS a finding
evidence_required: to report: an unguarded initialize() on a proxy/implementation that can be called by anyone and grants ownership
guarded initialize + atomic deployment is a negative finding
verification_evidence: OZ upgrades docs; Foundry: call initialize twice, second reverts.
root_cause: Unsafe variant of this pattern (state-after-call, no guard, unchecked result, unguarded privilege, no domain/nonce, non-atomic init, or unverified upgrade target) is what produces the vulnerability; the SAFE version shown here is the negative/FP reference.

title: Signature verification (EIP-712 + nonce + chainid)
mechanism: Signed data is hashed with a domain separator (name, version, chainid, verifying contract), bound to a per-signer nonce, and recovered via ECDSA; the recovered signer must match the expected principal and the nonce must be consumed atomically.
required_assumptions: domain separator includes chainid and verifying-contract address
every use consumes a fresh nonce atomically
recover verifies v/r/s malleability (ecrecover must be guarded or use OZ ECDSA)
why_safe: The signature is bound to this chain/contract and one-shot nonce, so it cannot be replayed elsewhere or twice.
known_limitations: does not protect a static (chainid-less) domain separator used across chains
signature replay after contract redeploy requires the nonce/domain to reset safely
gas-griefing via invalid signatures is still possible (checked last)
fp_patterns: a correctly domain-separated + nonced permit is safe
signature malleability is only a finding when the v/r/s check is missing
an EIP-712 domain WITHOUT chainid is a real finding only if the contract exists on multiple chains
evidence_required: to report: missing chainid/domain binding or a reused nonce, or an ecrecover without malleability protection
standard OZ ECDSA + nonce + chainid domain is a negative finding
verification_evidence: EIP-712 spec; Foundry: replay the same signature on another chain/address fails.
root_cause: Unsafe variant of this pattern (state-after-call, no guard, unchecked result, unguarded privilege, no domain/nonce, non-atomic init, or unverified upgrade target) is what produces the vulnerability; the SAFE version shown here is the negative/FP reference.

title: Secure upgrade patterns (storage layout, timelock, verified target)
mechanism: Upgrades are safe when the new implementation preserves storage layout (no slot collisions), the target is verified/immutable-approved, and the upgrade is authorized + timelocked so a malicious or accidental upgrade cannot land instantly.
required_assumptions: new implementation keeps the same storage layout (tool-verified)
the upgrade target is pre-verified/allowlisted
upgrade authority is protected and (ideally) delayed by a timelock
why_safe: A verified, timelocked, layout-compatible upgrade cannot be front-run to a malicious implementation and cannot silently corrupt storage.
known_limitations: storage-layout compatibility is a developer obligation (tooling helps, doesn't enforce at runtime)
does not protect against a compromised owner/upgrade key
selfdestruct in an old implementation bricks upgrades (Parity-style)
fp_patterns: a delegatecall into a VERIFIED, immutably-pinned logic contract is NOT by itself a vulnerability
an upgrade path with a timelock + verification is safe design, not a finding
a delegatecall into an arbitrary caller-controlled target IS a finding
evidence_required: to report delegatecall/upgrade: show an UNVERIFIED or caller-influenced target, or a storage-layout collision
verified target + immutable logic + timelock is a negative finding
verification_evidence: OZ upgrades docs; foundry-slot tests verify no storage collision after upgrade.

source: Solidity docs + OZ — false-positive guidance for low-level calls
title: Low-level calls are NOT automatically vulnerabilities
mechanism: address.call/delegatecall/transfer are legitimate tools; a finding requires a demonstrable flaw (unchecked result that matters, arbitrary target, state corruption), not the mere presence of the call.
required_assumptions: the call result is checked when it can affect protocol state
the target is not attacker-controlled for delegatecall
failure handling is explicit (revert or graceful path)
why_safe: A checked call with an explicit failure path cannot silently corrupt state; a fixed verified delegatecall target cannot be swapped to malicious code.
known_limitations: unchecked return in a loop that pays many users can grief (one failing recipient bricks the loop)
delegatecall to a library that can selfdestruct is a real risk (Parity)
gas forwarding to arbitrary recipients can fail
fp_patterns: a call() with require(ok) is NOT an unhandled-return finding
a delegatecall to a hard-coded, verified, audited library is NOT a delegatecall vulnerability
transfer() with fixed 2300 gas is a design choice, NOT a vulnerability by itself (griefing only with a batch loop)
evidence_required: to report unhandled-return: show the unchecked result feeds a later state write or a batch loop with a revert-bricking recipient
to report delegatecall: show an attacker-controlled/unverified target OR selfdestruct reachability
nothing else is sufficient
verification_evidence: Solidity docs; reproduce an unchecked-return failure in Foundry and observe the ledger corruption.
